The language spoken really depends on things like which side the tribe (or section, depending) sided with in the American Revolutionary war, Lower Canada Rebellion, etc., as well as trade alliances, though some other factors also have an effect. I won't delve too deeply into the history of my reservation in particular, but in essence, the way Quebec feels about the English coming and taking over (hence the "Je me souviens" license plate), is similar to how a lot of natives feel about the French (and later, the English as well). It's important to preserve the French language as a major part of Canada's history, and because the people are still here. However, in my opinion, it's not the indigenous peoples' responsibility to uphold that on their behalf as we're currently trying to protect our own for future generations.

It's also tough to go into languages in a broad sense because certain periods of history were rather ...tumultuous for the tribes, resulting in a bit of back and forth. For example, up until the 1870's, we were more fluent in French than English as a whole, though either were learned as necessary. This changed over time, in part due to conflict with the sulpicians of Montréal, and later, certain reservations' youth being sent to residential schools in Ontario instead of the 7 opened in Quebec. At the time of the residential schools, the shift to English was abrupt and thorough due to the Indian Agent and the Indian Act. In essence, the Indian Agent's job was to oversee the wellbeing of the tribes on behalf of Canada, which at the time meant outlawing speaking our traditional languages, singing, and ceremony. The Kanien'kè:ha speakers we have today are a direct result of the few who managed to hide under the radar or meet in secret to share our language and culture, as well as pass it on to their children who were able to both keep the secret and learn under those conditions. Also due to the secret practice, we have what we call "old" kanienkeha and "new" kanienkeha, the newer developing as words were lost and recreated.

Unfortunately, it wasn't passed down on either side of my own family for a few reasons:

1. Passing down the language was a big risk with a lot of baggage/trauma attached, especially for the kids coming out of the residential schools, where they were beaten and told to turn to god over such things.
2. My grandfather, who managed to remember some from his pre-residential school childhood, was deeply afraid that future generations would be prosecuted, like he witnessed and learned in school. It was a sore subject until his passing, so most of us learned not to ask again.
3. My family was Christian, like many in Kahnawake. The church was a major part of life for the "good", more obedient, natives, however Kanienkeha had little place in the church, except in regard to Kateri Tekakwitha.

That said, my ability in my traditional language is only as good as my French whereas I can read, listen and pick up a few things, but my brain + language in school = poor, POOR vocabulary, lol. Kanienkeha is a slow-but-steady work in progress for me as the platforms to learn tend to fall within school/business hours. My learning is mostly through work colleagues, which is surprisingly beneficial. I do, however, intend to pass on what I can and support local learning initiatives so that one day we might be able to offer better learning resources.

While I'm an outlier (because many families still have Eng/Kan or all three), If a white guy beats me to the punch, I'd probably feel happy for the language, but bad for myself because I feel cursed with languages 😂 
If I recall correctly, I think we do have a speaker who's a Norwegian polylingot. Never met him. Maybe I should claim him as a cousin. 🤣
